To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the statistical performance and computational efficiency are conflicting objectives in sparse principal component detection and that a trade-off between the two objectives exists.
(i) a computationally efficient test can detect signals of strength $\Theta(\sqrt{p\log n})$; (ii) no computationally efficient test exists that can detect signals of smaller strength.

1) the planted sparse principal component model can be solved by a polynomial-time SDP-based algorithm; 2) the planted sparse PCA model is hard to solve for polynomial-time algorithms, unless the planted clique problem can be solved efficiently; and 3) the planted sparse component model cannot be solved efficiently by any polynomial time algorithm unless P=NP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How does the computational efficiency of a test affect its statistical performance?
the question of how the statistical performance of an efficient algorithm is related to its computational complexity.
the question of whether it is possible to efficiently detect a sparse principal component in a high-dimensional data set, and if so, how well can it be done.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the statistical performance cannot be improved by any algorithm that runs in time polynomial in the number of samples.
the computational complexity of a statistical problem is closely linked to its performance, at least in the sparse principal component detection setting.
, in the planted clique model, if the planted clique problem is hard, then the sparse PCA detection is also hard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the statistical and computational efficiency are two sides of the same coin.
the statistical price to pay is the same as the computational price to pay.
the statistical price to pay is the computational price to pay.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for some problems in statistics, there is a tradeoff between the computational and statistical performance of an estimator.
the computational efficiency of a method may have a negative impact on its performance.
there is a trade-off between the statistical performance of a test and its computational complexity.
